featured_reviews.review_text:
we did the essential Mumbai tour with Parvez. he was a great guide for a great trip. The tour started off near the Asiatic society, and we walked around the area originally inside the Fort walls. He helped create a wonderful imagery of what the city looked like when it was founded along with some stories about the history before hand that led up to establishing Mumbai.
The trip was a mixture of walking and getting in and out of a car to see various sites around the city. It was quite varied and allowed us to see some unusual sites we would not have seen by ourselves.
at the end of the tour, we stopped at a restaurant with Parvez and tried several dishes that were excellent. Common food that is regularly served in restaurants, but this was delicious.

If this was representative of the companies tou, I would strongly recommend them for a tour.

featured_reviews.review_text:

We met Mr. Mickey, who led the walk, such an amazing, lively and knowledgeable guy. He kept the whole walk so engaging, the way he explained us about the things was truly outstanding. featured_reviews.review_text:
Must do -- even if you are a local!

featured_reviews.name: Tejal Samant
featured_reviews.review_text: We visited the BMC Headquarters with Khaki Tours on 25th May, and it was an absolutely awesome experience! The heritage architecture of the building is simply stunning — a true gem in the heart of Mumbai. Every Mumbaikar should and must visit this iconic place to appreciate the city's rich history and civic pride. Our tour guide, Juzer Tambawalla, was incredibly knowledgeable and engaging, bringing the stories of this magnificent structure to life. Highly recommended!

featured_reviews.name: P K
featured_reviews.review_text: We had arranged for a group tour of Castle 2 Gateway through Khakee Tour. It was the best experience we ever had. We had 55 people in group most of them born and bought up in Mumbai. But we didnt knew even 10% history and facts of what they showed and explained us. We had 3 sub groups but everybody had excellent experience with their guides. Our tour guide was Parag who was fabulous. His passion for Mumbai was evident. A must do tour for every mumbaikar

featured_reviews.name: Max Mackie
featured_reviews.review_text:
Mumbai history comes alive! An amazing walk with Surabhi.

I recently took the Fort area heritage walk with Khaki Tours, and I cannot recommend it enough. Our guide, Surabhi, was absolutely fantastic.
It wasn’t just a recitation of dates and facts; Surabhi is a natural storyteller. She wove together the history of colonial Bombay with fascinating anecdotes about the architecture and the people who built this city. She pointed out hidden details in the Gothic buildings that I would have walked right past without noticing.

Her energy was contagious, and she was incredibly patient in answering all our questions. Whether you are a tourist or a local Mumbaikar, you will see the Fort area with completely new eyes after this. If you book a Khaki Tour, definitely ask for Surabhi!

featured_reviews.review_text:
The Western Railway Heritage Gallery is a small but interesting place to visit in Mumbai. It’s located right opposite Churchgate station, so it’s very easy to find.Inside, you’ll get to see the history of Indian Railways through old tickets, vintage photographs, tools, and train models. Everything is displayed in a simple and neat way, so it doesn’t feel overwhelming or boring. One of the best things is that the entry is completely free.
Overall, it’s not a very big place, but it’s informative and worth visiting.

featured_reviews.name: Mallika Jamy
featured_reviews.review_text:
A tourist in my own city.
I bet Mumbai people have no idea about this gallery just opposite Churchgate station, this huge building that houses the Western Railway Heritage Gallery with history of railway in India.
The guard at the entrance is not of must help as no one visits this place, it's the Western Railway Headquarter but also has a small gallery on the ground floor.
Just step inside the main building and then take a left and the gallery starts with the history of Indian Railway, crockery, signalling equipments communication equipments, bells, tickets, old station photograph etc.
The interior looks magnificent with old architecture, flooring, roof design.
One can spend a good 20 minutes inside and leave.

You can ask the staff for directions in case of any confusion, because due to lack of foot falls, the staff usually keeps the lights inside the museum off, in order to save the electricity. featured_reviews.review_text:
A nice railway museum of Indian Railways history. A nice glimpse into the past of how private and princely states railways, eventually merged in the British era.
Among other interesting artefacts, it was a revelation to learn that sliverware dishes were used in railways catering during the Indian Raj days.
Good mix of Indian railways history and how railway technology around switching, signal and locomotive has evolved over the 2 centuries.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Rajabai Tower, University of Mumbai: The Mumbai University is undoubtedly one of the finest examples of Victorian Neo Gothic
Architecture in Mumbai. It is also an integral part of one of the finest urban ensembles of Victorian buildings in the world. The Rajabai Tower, with its imposing skyline, dominates the skyline of the Fort area, thus further strengthening its classification for reasons of scenic value.
The Mumbai University, designed by Sir Gilbert Scott, is an example of a public project in the city funded by local philanthropists, in this case, the "Cotton King" of Bombay, Premchund Roychund who made a generous contribution of Rupees 4 lakhs towards its construction. As a gesture of acknowledgment, the lofty Rajabai Tower, an awesome structure that rose to a height of 260 feet, was named after his mother. The Library structure adjoining the Rajabai Tower has among the finest ensembles of stained glass in the country while the splendid cross vaulted roof of the Reading Room with its polished timber members, is among the most spectacular architectural interiors in the city.

featured_reviews.review_text: Visited Rajabai Clock Tower and it’s a beautiful example of Gothic architecture in Mumbai. The intricate design and tall structure make it stand out in the Fort area. featured_reviews.name: lalit sonawane
featured_reviews.review_text: The Rajabai Clock Tower, located within the Fort campus of the University of Mumbai, is a magnificent blend of Gothic and Venetian architecture. Built in 1878, it stands as a historical landmark and one of Mumbai's iconic structures. The 85-meter-tall tower is adorned with exquisite stained glass windows and intricate carvings, making it a treat for architecture enthusiasts. Named after Rajabai, the mother of its patron, Premchand Roychand, the tower is not only a testament to Mumbai's colonial heritage but also a functioning clock tower. It offers picturesque views and is a must-visit for history lovers and tourists exploring the city's cultural landmarks.

The area around it is nice and peaceful, especially in the morning. If you love history and architecture, you’ll definitely like this place. It’s a great spot to check out while exploring South Mumbai!

featured_reviews.name: Rahul
featured_reviews.review_text:
Beautiful place which is seen from city
The 142-year-old Rajabai Clock Tower in South Mumbai’s Fort area, located inside University of Mumbai’s campus, is iconic for its Victorian-Gothic architecture. Built in 1878 by architect Sir George Gilbert Scott, it was commissioned by businessman Premchand Roychand as a tribute to his mother, hence the name. For years, it was the city’s tallest structure, at 285 feet. Rajabai Clock Tower has long been a beacon of the Oval Maidan precinct, a visual delight, and a valuable piece of history for the city. After brilliant restoration work by SNK Consultants, the clock tower was handed over to KSA Lighting Designers in 2017 for lighting the tower, the facade and the interiors of the University Library. Kanchan Puri, principal at the firm, tells us the process of this massive undertaking that was completed recently. After years of darkness, the Rajabai Clock Tower finally glowed up in 2021, literally.

featured_reviews.name: Amy
featured_reviews.review_text:
Review of South Mumbai

South Mumbai, often called the heart of the city, is where history, luxury, and urban life blend seamlessly. From colonial-era architecture to upscale shopping streets and breathtaking sea views, this part of the city offers a unique charm that sets it apart.

Architecture & Heritage

One of South Mumbai’s biggest draws is its stunning architecture. Landmarks like the Gateway of India, Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Terminus (CSMT), Bombay High Court, and the Taj Mahal Palace Hotel reflect the city’s rich colonial past. The area is a paradise for history lovers, with well-preserved Victorian-era buildings giving it a distinct old-world charm.

Culture & Lifestyle

South Mumbai is home to art galleries, theaters, museums, and cultural hubs. Places like Kala Ghoda, Jehangir Art Gallery, and the National Gallery of Modern Art attract art enthusiasts, while Marine Drive and Girgaum Chowpatty offer a peaceful retreat by the Arabian Sea. The nightlife here is vibrant, with high-end bars, clubs, and fine-dining restaurants.

Shopping & Dining

From the luxury boutiques of Colaba and Palladium Mall to the street shopping at Fashion Street and Crawford Market, South Mumbai caters to all kinds of shoppers. The dining scene is equally diverse, offering everything from iconic Irani cafés like Kyani & Co. to fine-dining establishments like The Table and Wasabi by Morimoto.

Transport & Accessibility

South Mumbai is well-connected by local trains, buses, and taxis, but traffic congestion can be a major issue, especially during peak hours. The Mumbai Metro expansion is expected to improve connectivity in the future.

Overall Experience

South Mumbai is where Mumbai’s heritage, culture, and modern luxury come together. Whether you’re a history buff, a foodie, a shopaholic, or just someone who enjoys a scenic sunset by the sea, this part of the city has something for everyone.

Rating: 4.8/5
A must-visit area that captures the true essence of Mumbai, though traffic and high costs can be a drawback!

featured_reviews.name: Ritesh K R
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visited the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya recently, and while the permanent collections are always impressive, what truly stood out this time were the special exhibitions currently on display—deeply immersive, contemporary, and culturally rooted.

The “Roots of a City: The Pathare Prabhus of Mumbai” exhibition is incredibly intimate. Instead of telling history through grand events, it brings together family heirlooms, photographs, recipes, and everyday objects to narrate the story of one of Mumbai’s oldest communities. It feels less like a museum display and more like stepping into someone’s living memory—quiet, layered, and deeply human.

The “Metamorphosis II” exhibition offers a striking contrast—more interpretive and artistic—exploring transformation through textiles, craft, and visual storytelling. The curation feels thoughtful and contemporary, making traditional practices feel alive and evolving rather than static.

I also really appreciated the installation work (including pieces like Navjot Altaf’s environmental/art narratives such as “Waste archives as Landscapes ”), which added a powerful social and ecological lens to the overall experience—pushing you to reflect, not just observe.

Overall, what makes CSMVS special right now is how it balances:History + personal memory,
Craft + contemporary interpretation, Heritage + social commentary

The museum itself, with its Indo-Saracenic architecture and vast collection of ~50,000 artefacts, remains one of Mumbai’s cultural anchors—but these exhibitions elevate it into something far more dynamic and relevant today.

If you’re in Mumbai, don’t just go for the main galleries—make time for the temporary exhibitions. They’re the real highlight right now.

featured_reviews.review_text:
Hutatma Chowk is located in the busy financial district of Fort. It derives its present name from an incident in 1956 when a peaceful demonstration by the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti (United Maharashtra Committee) was fired upon by the police resulting in 106 deaths. The incident was part of ongoing struggles of the Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti, amongst others, for the creation of the State of Maharashtra. The shooting proved to be a major impetus for the creation of Maharashtra on 1 May 1960.

The Hutatma Chowk square is lined on all sides by buildings constructed during the British Raj. An ornate fountain surrounded by delicately carved figures forms the center of the huge square. This was the Flora Fountain.

The fountain itself was built in 1864 and represents the Roman Goddess Flora, the Goddess of Abundance. Today, it is a heritage structure. It cost Rs. 47,000 to build, a large sum at the time, and was constructed by the Agri-Horticultural Society of Western India. Cursetjee Fardoonjee Parekh donated Rs.20,000 towards the construction of this fountain. The fountain was carved from stone that was imported from Portland. It was built in honour of Sir Bartle Frere, who was the Governor of Bombay at the time. Sir Bartle was responsible for dismantling Bombay Fort and shaping much of modern Mumbai. Initially it was to be named after the Governor but the name was changed before the fountain was unveiled. When it was constructed, it was in the middle of the city. Flora fountain stands in exactly the same place where the original Churchgate of Bombay Fort stood. The area around Flora Fountain is the business center of Mumbai and is surrounded by offices, banks, colleges and shops.

This is usually part of stops during heritage walks.

The Hutatma Memorial Statue, located at Hutatma Chowk in South Mumbai, stands as a powerful symbol of sacrifice and courage. This historic landmark commemorates the martyrs who laid down their lives during the Samyukta Maharashtra Movement in 1956, fighting for the formation of a separate Marathi-speaking state. The memorial features two tall white stone pillars with eternal flames at the top, representing the spirit and bravery of the fallen heroes.

Surrounded by some of Mumbai’s busiest roads, the memorial creates a striking contrast between the city’s fast-paced life and the deep history it represents. Despite constant traffic, the area maintains a sense of solemnity and respect. Many people pause here—whether briefly or intentionally—to reflect on the sacrifices made for Maharashtra’s identity.

The statue is especially significant for locals and history enthusiasts, as it reminds citizens of the struggles behind the state’s formation. At night, the memorial is beautifully lit, enhancing its emotional impact and making it visually striking. The nearby Flora Fountain adds to the historic charm of the location.

While it is not a tourist attraction in the conventional sense, the Hutatma Memorial holds immense cultural and emotional value. It serves as a reminder that modern Mumbai stands on the sacrifices of brave individuals whose voices shaped history. Visiting this memorial instills a sense of pride, respect, and responsibility toward preserving the legacy of Maharashtra’s freedom fighters.

The square is a popular and touristy spot as it’s close to all the main sights of Mumbai and also has the lovely Flora Fountain.
The square hosts Flora Fountain and was known by that name until 1960. It was officially renamed in 1960 in memory of the members of Samyukta Maharashtra Samiti, who lost their lives when police fired upon their peaceful demonstration. A statue of a "Martyr with a Flame" stands next to Flora Fountain.
Apart from the statue and the fountain, the entire area is filled with buildings and structures constructed during the Britain’s colonization of the country. A must visit when in Mumbai.
You can see beautiful Flora Fountain just behind the memorial statue. This is the place where you can find amazing shots for your photos and find the beautiful heritage buildings also. You can buy book just walkable distance & it’s known as FORT Books Lane.

featured_reviews.review_text:
🏛️ Churchgate Station & Heritage Building – A Glimpse of Timeless Mumbai
Right at the third stop during our visit, we reached the iconic Churchgate Railway Station area, and it instantly felt like stepping into a different era. The British-era architecture, beautifully preserved and maintained, stands tall as a reminder of Mumbai’s rich colonial past.
The building, especially at night, looked absolutely stunning with warm, golden lighting highlighting its intricate design, domes, and structure. Every corner reflects attention to detail—from the stonework to the symmetry—making it a visual treat for anyone who appreciates heritage architecture.
What truly stands out is how well the place has been maintained in its original charm, yet seamlessly integrated into the hustle of modern Mumbai. Even amidst the city’s fast pace, this structure holds a calm, dignified presence.
The surroundings were lively yet not chaotic:
A steady movement of people
Vehicles passing by in rhythm
The building glowing as a silent witness to decades of history
It’s not just a railway station area—it’s a living landmark, representing the evolution of Mumbai from its colonial roots to today’s metropolitan identity.
Overall Experience:
A perfect blend of history, architecture, and urban life, especially mesmerizing at night.
⭐ Rating: 5/5
✔️ Beautifully preserved heritage
✔️ Excellent night lighting
✔️ Iconic Mumbai landmark
✔️ Great for quick stops and photography
If you’re exploring South Mumbai, Churchgate is not just a transit point—it’s an experience in itself.

featured_reviews.name: Rahul Kurup
featured_reviews.review_text:
The heartbeat of South Mumbai! 🚉💙
Churchgate isn't just a station; it’s an absolute vibe. If you want to see the real 'Mumbai Spirit' in action, this is the place. It’s the final stop, so you actually have a chance of getting a seat before the madness begins! 🏃💨
The Good Stuff:
✅ Clean & Organized: Surprisingly well-maintained for such a busy hub.
✅ Seamless Metro Link: The new Metro Line 3 connection is a game-changer for getting around.
✅ Iconic Location: Walk out and you’re minutes away from Marine Drive for that post-work sunset, or hitting up the legendary food stalls nearby. 🍦🌊
✅ Accessibility: Escalators and elevators actually work!
Pro Tip: If you’re a tourist, stand near the tracks during the afternoon to watch the Dabbawalas do their legendary lunchbox sorting—it’s like a synchronized dance. 🍱
It can get chaotic during rush hour (standard Mumbai rules apply: keep moving or get moved!), but there’s no better gateway to the city.
10/10 would catch a fast train from here again. ✌️

featured_reviews.name: Akshay Karve
featured_reviews.review_text:
Churchgate Station is one of the best-maintained suburban railway stations in Mumbai and easily earns a 4 out of 5 rating. The station has multiple spacious platforms that are relatively well-organized, making boarding and deboarding smoother even during peak hours. Signage across platforms and exits is clear, which helps both daily commuters and occasional visitors navigate without much confusion.
Cleanliness is noticeably better compared to many other stations in the city, with regular maintenance and less littering on platforms. There are adequate ticketing counters as well as ATVM machines, which help reduce long queues, although rush hours can still be hectic.
The station also offers a variety of small shops, food stalls, and kiosks for quick snacks, beverages, and essentials. Facilities like seating areas, drinking water, and basic washrooms are available, though washroom hygiene can still be improved.
Multiple exits make it convenient to access different parts of South Mumbai, and the connectivity to taxis, buses, and nearby offices is excellent. Overall, Churchgate Station provides a smooth, efficient, and fairly comfortable travel experience despite heavy daily footfall.

featured_reviews.name: Vijender Singh
featured_reviews.review_text:
Churchgate Station : Clean, Busy and Very Convenient

Churchgate Station is well maintained and one of the most organised stations in Mumbai. It’s very close to Marine Drive - just a short walk away which makes it easy for tourists and office-goers. Trains run smoothly every 2–3 minutes to different parts of the city so you never have to wait too long.

The platforms are clean, the signboards are clear and there’s good crowd management during peak hours. Outside the station, you’ll find plenty of taxis, buses and food stalls. It’s also a major starting point for exploring South Mumbai including Nariman Point, Colaba and Fort area.

A reliable and convenient station whether you're commuting daily or visiting the area.

featured_reviews.name: Anil Yadav
featured_reviews.review_text: Churchgate Station is the bustling, iconic southern terminal of Mumbai's Western Line, offering easy access to Nariman Point, Marine Drive, and tourist spots. As a heritage site, it has a charming, old-world exterior but is intensely crowded with daily commuters, making it a high-energy, "mad rush" experience during peak hours.

featured_reviews.name: Ansuman Bag
featured_reviews.review_text: Churchgate Station is an iconic and historic landmark that serves as the ultimate gateway to South Mumbai. As a major terminus, it handles an incredible volume of daily commuters with surprising efficiency. The station premises are well-maintained, remarkably clean, and feature clear signage that makes navigating the heavy peak-hour rush manageable. Food stalls, ticketing counters, and basic amenities are easily accessible. Its location is unbeatable—stepping right outside connects you directly to top colleges, corporate hubs, and it’s just a scenic stroll away from Marine Drive.

featured_reviews.name: Parva Dave
featured_reviews.review_text: Churchgate Station is one of the best railway stations in Mumbai. It is clean, well-maintained, and well-connected to different parts of the city. The station has clear signboards, good security, and plenty of facilities for commuters. Trains are frequent, making travel convenient and efficient. The surrounding area is lively, with easy access to colleges, offices, and tourist attractions. Overall, a great station that provides a smooth and comfortable travel experience. Highly recommended!

The Heart of Mumbai's Cricket and Heritage!

"Oval Maidan is a vast and vital green space in the Fort area, providing a much-needed open area in the busy South Mumbai.

It is most famous for its role in Mumbai's cricket scene, with countless matches being played simultaneously, especially on weekends.

It is a fantastic place to witness the city's passion for the sport.

The Maidan is bordered by stunning Victorian Gothic and Art Deco architecture, including the Bombay High Court and the University of Mumbai, which makes for a beautiful and historic backdrop.

It serves as an excellent spot for a morning run, an evening stroll, or just relaxing under the shade of a tree.

While it can get busy, the Oval Maidan is essential to the city's spirit and a perfect place to experience local life and admire Mumbai's rich architectural heritage."

featured_reviews.name: Sakib Mulla
featured_reviews.review_text:
Occupying a majestic 22-acre expanse in the heart of South Mumbai,the Oval Maidan is a sublime palimpsest of colonial grandeur and contemporary leisure. Enveloped by the architectural duality of the Victorian Gothic revival to the east and the sleek Art Deco ensembles to the west now collectively enshrined as a UNESCO World Heritage site the ground serves as a verdant bridge between centuries.
To traverse its periphery is to witness a sophisticated choreography of Mumbai’s social fabric. Under the watchful shadow of the Rajabai Clock Tower, the air is thick with the rhythmic thwack of willow against leather, as aspiring cricketers populate the dusty pitches in a relentless pursuit of sporting excellence. The maidan functions as a civic lung, exhaling a serene tranquility that contrasts sharply with the frantic kinesis of nearby Churchgate.
The aesthetic appeal lies in its unmanicured authenticity; it is neither a rigid botanical garden nor a chaotic wasteland, but a curated void that permits the city to breathe. As the golden hour bathes the limestone gargoyles of the High Court in amber hues, the Maidan transcends its physical boundaries, becoming a temporal sanctuary. It is an indispensable urban theater where history remains a living, breathing participant in the everyday life of the metropolis. For the discerning visitor, it offers a peerless vantage point to observe the architectural and cultural heartbeat of Mumbai.

Given the crowds, the ground is decently well maintained and clean.

featured_reviews.name: Vivek Vetal
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visiting St. Thomas Cathedral in Fort, Mumbai felt less like ticking off a heritage checklist and more like stepping into a quieter, more reflective version of the city—one that still breathes calmly despite the chaos outside. Tucked amidst the rush of office-goers, traffic signals, and colonial-era buildings, the cathedral stands with a grace that doesn’t demand attention, yet effortlessly commands respect.

What struck me first was the sense of calm the moment I entered the premises. The noise of Fort seemed to fade instantly, replaced by a soft stillness that felt almost therapeutic. It’s rare to find such a space in South Mumbai where time seems to slow down, inviting you to pause, observe, and simply be present. The cathedral isn’t just visually beautiful; it has an emotional weight to it—one that gently nudges you towards introspection.

The architecture is understated yet powerful. There’s no excessive ornamentation, but every element feels purposeful. The high ceilings, elegant arches, and stained-glass windows allow natural light to pour in, creating an atmosphere that feels warm and welcoming rather than intimidating. As sunlight filters through the glass, the interiors take on a soft glow, making it an ideal place to sit quietly, even if only for a few minutes.

What I appreciated most was how alive the space feels, despite its age. This isn’t a museum frozen in time; it’s a living landmark that continues to serve as a place of worship, community, and history. Reading the plaques and memorials, you’re reminded of the countless lives and stories that have passed through these walls—stories of colonial Bombay, changing times, and enduring faith.

St. Thomas Cathedral is not just for those interested in religion or history. It’s for anyone seeking a moment of calm, a connection to Mumbai’s layered past, or simply a peaceful corner to gather their thoughts. Every visit leaves you a little lighter, a little calmer, and with a renewed appreciation for the quieter, soulful side of the city.

featured_reviews.name: Foodieextreme Foodieextreme
featured_reviews.review_text:
Visited July 15, 2025 – Day 12 in India

After visiting the Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj Vastu Sangrahalaya museum, our guide brought us to St. Thomas Cathedral—a beautiful and deeply historic church nestled in the heart of Mumbai. Built in the early 1700s, it’s the city’s oldest Anglican church and feels like a peaceful sanctuary surrounded by history.

What took me by surprise were the many graves laid directly into the floor. I made sure my husband and our daughters, ages five and seven, were careful not to step on any. My girls noticed a small white grave and were curious if it belonged to a child. When we read the inscription, we saw that it was for a 54-year-old woman, the wife of an officer. That moment sparked quiet reflection and curiosity in all of us.

Inside, we saw the seat where Mother Teresa had once sat, which was marked with a small plaque. Nearby were two elegant seats once used by King George V and Queen Mary during their visit in 1911. My husband and daughters loved the experience of sitting in those very seats, imagining what it must have been like over a century ago.

What I personally loved most was the peace I felt in the church. Before this trip, many people had asked me to pray for them, knowing this journey was meaningful to me on a spiritual level. In the stillness of the cathedral, I took time to sit quietly and pray for each of them. It was a heartfelt and emotional experience.

featured_reviews.review_text:
St. Thomas’ Cathedral is one of Mumbai’s most historic and beautiful churches, offering a serene escape in the bustling Fort area. Built in 1718, it is the oldest Anglican church in Mumbai and an essential part of the city's colonial heritage. The church, now part of the Church of North India (C.N.I.), is not just a place of worship but also a significant historical monument.

Historical Importance: As Mumbai’s first Anglican church, St. Thomas’ Cathedral played a crucial role in the city's colonial past. It was built during British rule and remains a testament to the city's rich history.
Stunning Architecture: The church features classic Neo-Gothic and colonial architectural styles, with elegant arches, stained glass windows, and intricate carvings that transport you back in time.
Peaceful Ambience: Despite being in the heart of the bustling Fort area, the church’s interiors are calm and soothing, making it a perfect place for reflection and prayer.
Well-Preserved Memorials: The walls of the cathedral are adorned with memorial plaques dedicated to British soldiers and officers, offering a glimpse into Mumbai’s past.
UNESCO Recognition: The cathedral is a part of the Victorian Gothic and Art Deco Ensemble of Mumbai, which has been recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Visiting Experience
Best Time to Visit: Morning hours are ideal for a quiet and spiritual experience. The church is open to visitors on most days.

Surroundings: Located near Horniman Circle, it is close to landmarks like Flora Fountain, Bombay High Court, Rajabai Clock Tower, and the Asiatic Library.

Mass Timings: If you wish to attend a service, check their schedule beforehand, as Sunday Mass is particularly special.

Photography: While photography is allowed in most areas, it’s best to be respectful as it is an active place of worship.

St. Thomas’ Cathedral is a must-visit for history buffs, architecture lovers, and anyone looking for a moment of peace in Mumbai’s fast-paced environment. Whether you admire its heritage, attend a service, or simply enjoy its quiet beauty, this cathedral is truly a hidden treasure in Mumbai.

featured_reviews.name: Derishta Pillay
featured_reviews.review_text:
At the outset I must say that neither myself nor my husband are huge fans of the usual guided walking tours mainly because we hate being taken to cliched and crowded tourist hotspots, listening to facts straight from the Wikipedia page and jostling for space with other tourists just to return sunburned and underwhelmed. In addition we'd already spent a hectic 5 weeks in India - we were tired, grumpy, waiting to fly back home and not at all looking forward to our last 4 days in Mumbai at all. So basically when our travel companions insisted we book a tour - the scene was set for disaster...
'Bombay Walks' single handedly turned this around and Mumbai actually turned out to be the highlight of our trip! (Nope this is not a sponsored review 😂)

The tour: Arpan's tour extends to the days before and after the actual tour as he offers valuable advice about where to stay/eat/party/shop etc. He speaks perfect English, is pleasant and very easy to communicate with. His passion and love for the city is infectious and you will end his tour enthralled, overwhelmed and completely charmed by Mumbai and it's people - vowing to come back and dig deeper, spend longer and see more. The city tour covers many facets of the city - traveling to hidden gems and local landmarks across the length and breadth of Mumbai. You get to see and experience aspects of Mumbai that you'd never be able to do alone with a guide book or google maps - like traveling on local trains and walking through Worli fishing village and stopping by at small off-the-beaten path temples and churches.

The guide: Arpan is reliable, trustworthy and comes well prepared for the type of group. His talking style is light-hearted and easy going but still knowledgeable and always engaging. He's the type of guide that can tell you interesting facts about the history, architecture and politics of a place but also where to get the best coconut water along the way and which public toilets are ok to use.
We only met Arpan in person on the day of the tour and although we were constantly bombarded with sights, sounds and smells (it is Mumbai after all) - it never once felt like we were just being dragged from point to point whilst he rattled off information but rather that we were spending the day walking around with an old friend.

Target travelers: We're fairly well travelled and yet this is the first time we've ever bothered to leave a tour review - on any platform - I think that in itself indicates how highly we recommend this tour.
This is really a 'must do' in Mumbai.
It's so good we would do this tour again even if it were to cover the exact route we already took. The walking wasn't particular strenuous so it's recommended for any age group it should also be noted that we found that     Arpan was discreetly always conscious of where the group members were and their safety and constantly aware of our surroundings and the locals around us - on that note I would recommend this tour even if you're a single female traveling alone.

When to do it: Try and do this tour on your first full day in Mumbai because it's also a great way to orientate yourself around the city and plan the rest of your time there.

That city that everyone talks about - that's all of India's many faces and layers in one, that accepts everyone, that's everyone's home - regardless of language, religion or creed - Mumbai is THAT city and you'd be crazy if you miss the opportunity to let a born-and-bred local guide you around...

The Western Railway Headquarters is a beautiful piece of architecture that represents the rich history of the city's transportation industry. The building is well-maintained, and the grounds are kept clean and tidy. The staff is friendly and knowledgeable about the building's history, and they are always happy to answer any questions you may have.

Overall, I highly recommend a visit to the Western Railway Headquarters for anyone interested in the history of transportation in the city. It's a great place to learn about the city's past and see a beautiful piece of architecture.
The Western Railway Headquarters is a historic building located in Mumbai, India. It was built in 1930 and served as the administrative headquarters of the Western Railway until 2018.

The building was designed by the British architect William Emerson, who was also responsible for designing many other iconic buildings in Mumbai, including the Victoria Terminus (now known as the Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus) and the Crawford Market.

The Western Railway Headquarters building was constructed in the Art Deco style, which was popular during the 1920s and 1930s. The building is known for its distinctive façade, which features a series of vertical and horizontal lines, decorative motifs, and a clock tower.

Over the years, the building has played an important role in the city's transportation industry, serving as the nerve center of the Western Railway, which operates trains between Mumbai and various other destinations in western India.

In 2018, the Western Railway Headquarters was shifted to a new location, and the building is now being used for other purposes. However, it remains an important landmark in Mumbai's architectural history, and efforts are being made to preserve and maintain its distinctive Art Deco features.

featured_reviews.review_text:
The Western Railway Headquarters, located at Churchgate, South Mumbai, is one of the most prominent and historically significant railway buildings in the city. Situated on Maharshi Karve Road, close to the Arabian Sea, the building reflects a blend of colonial-era architecture and institutional grandeur. During the daytime, it appears solid and imposing with its symmetrical structure, wide frontage, and classic stone façade, symbolizing the administrative strength of Western Railway, which manages one of India’s busiest suburban rail networks.

At night, the Western Railway Headquarters looks especially beautiful and striking. The building is illuminated with warm lights that highlight its architectural details, arches, and vertical lines. The glow against the dark sky, combined with the nearby sea breeze and calm surroundings, creates a peaceful and elegant atmosphere. The proximity to Marine Drive’s Queen’s Necklace lighting further enhances the visual appeal, making the area attractive for evening walks and photography.

Reaching the Western Railway Headquarters is very convenient. Churchgate Railway Station, the terminal station of the Western Line, is located just opposite the building, at a walking distance of less than 100 meters. It is directly connected to Mumbai’s suburban railway network, making access easy from all parts of the city. From Marine Drive, the distance to the headquarters is approximately 1 to 1.2 kilometers, which can be covered in 10–15 minutes on foot or 5 minutes by car or taxi, depending on traffic. Several BEST buses, taxis, and app-based cab services also operate frequently in this area.
